summary: Where the prairie runs straight into the Rocky Mountains, in Alberta's south-west corner. Waterton's chain of lakes reaches across the border into Montana's Glacier National Park, with which it forms the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park. Walk to Bear's Hump above the Prince of Wales Hotel, see the red rock of Red Rock Canyon, or take the boat to the Crypt Lake trail. It is small, windy and full of wildflowers.
story: Waterton's mountains are old rock that travelled. The layers were laid down on the floor of an ancient sea about 1,500 million years ago, and ripple marks and salt-crystal casts are still visible in them. A single flat sheet of this rock then slid some 100 kilometres north-east over much younger, 70-million-year-old Cretaceous rock, along the fault called the Lewis Thrust. The red and green stone of Red Rock Canyon is argillite, coloured by oxidised and unoxidised iron. Ice carved the U-shaped valley of Upper Waterton Lake and the cirque that holds Cameron Lake; no glaciers remain in the park today.

The park is small, 505 square kilometres, but its four ecoregions, from foothills parkland to alpine, hold more than 1,000 kinds of vascular plants, over half of Alberta's plant species. It is the only national park in Canada protecting rough fescue grassland, and wildflowers fill the Blakiston Valley in June. Grizzly and black bears, elk, bighorn sheep and cougars live here, and a small herd of plains bison has grazed a paddock near the north boundary since 1952. It is also one of the windiest places in Canada, with Alberta's highest average precipitation and frequent winter chinooks.

Waterton lies within the traditional and sacred territory of the Siksikaitsitapi, the Blackfoot, who call the lake Paahtómahksikimi, the Sacred Lake within the Mountains. The lakes take their English name from the naturalist Charles Waterton, given by Lieutenant Blakiston of the Palliser Expedition. A rancher, F. W. Godsal, urged Ottawa to protect the area in 1893, and on 30 May 1895 a 140-square-kilometre Dominion Forest Park was set aside, Canada's fourth national park. Western Canada's first oil well was drilled here in 1902, and the Great Northern Railway opened the Prince of Wales Hotel in 1927.

In 1932, prompted by Alberta and Montana Rotarians, Canada and the United States joined Waterton and Glacier national parks as the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park, a World Heritage Site since 1995. In September 2017 the Kenow Wildfire, started by lightning in British Columbia, burned into the park on 11 September, swept through 19,303 hectares of it and destroyed the visitor centre and Crandell Mountain Campground. Over 80 per cent of the trail network was affected; the land has been regrowing since, and a new visitor centre now stands in the townsite.
howItWorks: Everyone travelling in the park needs a park pass, by order of the superintendent; only those driving straight through on Highways 5 or 6 without stopping are exempt. Youth aged 17 and under get in free. A daily pass, valid until 4 pm the next day, also covers Banff, Jasper, Yoho, Kootenay, Mount Revelstoke, Glacier and Elk Island national parks; Waterton also sells its own annual pass in person, and the Parks Canada Discovery Pass covers more than 80 Parks Canada places for twelve months. Under the Canada Strong Pass, admission was free for three periods in 2025 and 2026; the last ended on 7 September 2026 and regular fees apply again.

Townsite Campground, with 246 sites, is booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service from mid-May to late September, and first come, first served on its shoulder dates; Belly River Campground takes no reservations and often fills by early afternoon in July and August, and Crandell Mountain Campground remains closed. The nine backcountry campgrounds can be used only with a backcountry use permit for a specific site, booked online or at the visitor centre; carry a copy with you. Gas stoves are required for cooking, and fires are allowed only in the metal rings at five of them.

To keep out invasive mussels and whirling disease, non-motorised watercraft from outside the park, from canoes and paddleboards to inflatable loungers, may not be launched on any lake or river in Waterton; boats stored in the park can qualify for a seasonal permit after an inspection. Motorised and trailered boats go through a 90-day quarantine and sealing programme, and all other water equipment needs a self-certification permit. On land, stay 100 metres from bears, cougars and wolves and 30 metres from elk, deer, moose and bighorn sheep, keep a bare campsite, and carry bear spray. Recreational drones are prohibited, with fines up to $25,000.

sights.name: Bear's Hump
sights.note: A 2.8-kilometre return trail to one of the park's best-known viewpoints, starting across the Entrance Road from the Prince of Wales Hotel access road.

sights.name: Prince of Wales Hotel
sights.note: A chalet-style railway hotel with a timber-framed interior, opened by the Great Northern Railway in 1927 on a glacial kame above Upper Waterton Lake; a national historic site.

sights.name: Cameron Falls
sights.note: A waterfall in Waterton townsite on the townsite loop path, beside the trailhead of the Alderson–Carthew route.

sights.name: Red Rock Canyon
sights.note: A gorge of red and green argillite at the end of the 15-kilometre Red Rock Parkway, with a 0.7-kilometre loop trail. Open to cars May to late October.

sights.name: Cameron Lake
sights.note: A cirque lake at the end of the Akamina Parkway, whose southern end reaches across the border into Montana, with a 3-kilometre return lakeshore trail.

sights.name: Crypt Lake
sights.note: A 17.2-kilometre return day hike from a boat landing across Upper Waterton Lake, past waterfalls and through a tight tunnel onto a cliff ledge. Book the boat shuttle.

sights.name: Bertha Lake
sights.note: A mountain lake 10.4 kilometres return from the townsite, passing Lower Bertha Falls; the trailhead lies in an avalanche path, so check the daily Bertha-Townsite advisory.

sights.name: Upper Waterton Lake
sights.note: The lake in a glacier-carved valley that crosses the international border. The MV International, built in 1927, still carries boat tours on it.

sights.name: Waterton Lakes Visitor Centre
sights.note: The new Parks Canada centre at 404 Cameron Falls Drive, open all year, with permits, backcountry bookings, trail and avalanche reports, and exhibits on Blackfoot culture.

entrances: The park gate on the Entrance Parkway, which runs 8 kilometres from the Maskinonge wetlands past the gate to the townsite
The Chief Mountain Highway from the Chief Mountain border crossing with Montana, open seasonally
Waterton townsite, the base for the visitor centre, the boats on Upper Waterton Lake and most trailheads
planYourVisit.reservations: Townsite Campground is reservable from mid-May to late September through the Parks Canada Reservation Service; backcountry campgrounds are reservable from late May or late June to mid-October, and at other times through the visitor centre on 403-859-5133. Belly River Campground is first come, first served. Weekends in July and August are very busy and parking lots fill by 11 am. Check before you go with Parks Canada.
permits: Park pass for anyone travelling in the park, except through traffic on Highways 5 and 6
Backcountry use permit for every overnight trip, for named campgrounds
Self-certification permit for any water equipment; non-motorised boats from outside the park may not be launched
National park fishing permit; provincial licences are not valid
camping: Townsite Campground: 246 sites from full service to walk-in, no fire pits
Belly River Campground on the Chief Mountain Highway: basic sites, first come, first served, late May to early September
Nine backcountry campgrounds, among them Bertha Lake, Alderson Lake, Twin Lakes and Boundary Bay
lodging: The Prince of Wales Hotel and other private accommodation in Waterton townsite
Private campgrounds, provincial parks and other accommodation outside the park
seasonalClosures: The Red Rock Parkway is open to vehicles only from about May to late October
Beyond Little Prairie day-use area the Akamina Parkway closes to vehicles in winter
The Bison Paddock Loop Road is open from about mid-May to early November
The Chief Mountain border crossing is open about 15 May to 30 September, and the townsite's only fuel station closes in winter — check before you go with Parks Canada

weather: Waterton's weather is defined by moisture, wind and sudden change. Summers are short and generally cool, though highs can reach 35 °C, and nights can drop below freezing; rain, snow or hail can fall in any month. The average daily wind is 30 kilometres an hour, and in autumn and winter gusts over 100 are common. Winters are long but relatively mild: chinooks can lift the temperature above 10 °C in hours, though it can also fall to −40 °C. It is the wettest place in Alberta, with about 1,520 millimetres a year at Cameron Lake, much of it as snow. June brings the wildflowers; July and August are the busy season.
directions: Waterton townsite is 132 kilometres from Lethbridge, 271 kilometres from Calgary and 371 kilometres from Banff by paved road; the park entrance is off Highways 5 and 6. From Montana, the Chief Mountain Highway crosses the border 30 kilometres from the townsite and is open seasonally; the year-round crossings are Carway on Highway 2 south of Cardston and Roosville south of Fernie. Car hire is available in Calgary and Lethbridge. Fuel is sold in the townsite only in summer and has no diesel; the nearest year-round stations are in Pincher Creek and Mountain View. Check 511 Alberta or DriveBC before you go.

chronology.text: Pincher Creek rancher F. W. Godsal proposes to Ottawa that the Waterton Lakes be protected.
A 140-square-kilometre Dominion Forest Park is set aside on 30 May, Canada's fourth national park.
The first oil strike in western Canada, at Original Discovery No. 1 in the Cameron Valley.
John George 'Kootenai' Brown, the area's first settler, becomes the first park official.
The Prince of Wales Hotel opens on 25 July, and bus service to Glacier National Park begins.
Canada and the United States create the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park; Canada's bill passes on 16 June.
A herd of plains bison is established in the park's bison paddock.
Waterton becomes the core of Canada's second UNESCO biosphere reserve.
Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park is inscribed as a World Heritage Site on 6 December.
The Kenow Wildfire burns 19,303 hectares of the park in September and destroys the visitor centre.
Six plains bison from Elk Island return to the paddock in February, welcomed by Kainai, Piikani and Siksika Elders; the peace park becomes a certified International Dark Sky Park.

safety: Grizzly and black bears live throughout the park. Carry bear spray where you can reach it, make noise on the trail, and leave at once if you find a carcass.
The wind is strong and sudden. Upper Waterton Lake stays around 10–15 °C even in late summer, drops off quickly and can turn rough; wear a life jacket and get off the water if you hear thunder.
The Crypt Lake trail climbs steep slopes and passes through a tight tunnel onto a narrow ledge above a cliff; be sure you are comfortable with heights before you set out.
Mobile coverage is limited. In an emergency dial 911; report wildlife to Parks Canada Dispatch on 1-888-927-3367.
regulations: A park pass is required for everyone travelling in the park.
Non-motorised watercraft from outside the park may not be launched; all water equipment needs a self-certification permit, and motorised boats must be quarantined and sealed for 90 days first.
Stay 30 metres from elk, deer, moose and sheep and 100 metres from bears, cougars and wolves; feeding wildlife can bring a fine of up to $25,000.
Recreational drones are prohibited throughout the park.
Camp only in designated campgrounds with a permit, and in the backcountry only on the tent pads provided.
